challenges.note: Eight correct actions in a row

hazards.lift-alone-without-second-person: That's starting the lift without the second paraeducator in position. The plan calls for two people because a transfer that goes wrong partway through needs a second set of hands already there, not one being called for after the student is already off balance.
hazards.skip-gait-belt: That's reaching for an underarm hold instead of the gait belt. A grip under the arms has nothing to hold onto if the student's legs give way mid-transfer and can injure the shoulder it's pulling on — the gait belt is the one hold built to carry weight safely by design.
hazards.twist-while-lifting: That's a twist through the back instead of a pivot on the feet. A spine loaded and twisted at the same time is exactly the motion behind the injuries a lift-and-transfer job sees most — the feet turn to face the new seat; the back stays square to whatever it's carrying the whole way round.
hazards.unlocked-brake-attempt: The wheelchair's brakes were never actually locked, and the transfer is starting anyway. A chair that rolls even a few inches mid-transfer takes the base out from under a lift that was counting on it staying put.

interrupts.alert: Partway through the pivot, the student signals discomfort — this isn't going the way the plan expects.
interrupts.cue: Pause the pivot and check in before continuing.
interrupts.missNote: The pivot continued through a clear discomfort signal — a plan followed past the point where it stops matching what's actually happening is no longer the safe transfer it was written to be.
interrupts.why: A transfer plan describes what should happen, not a guarantee that it always will — signalled discomfort mid-pivot gets a pause and a check-in with the partner holding the other side, not a push through to finish the motion faster.
interrupts.wrongNote: Check in with your partner — that's what a discomfort signal mid-pivot calls for, not finishing the motion.

interrupts.alert: A classroom aide across the room is calling for help with an unrelated incident right as the transfer is about to start.
interrupts.cue: Stay with the transfer — it doesn't stop partway through for something else.
interrupts.kind: Classroom aide needs help across the room
interrupts.missNote: Attention went across the room mid-setup, and the transfer sat half-ready with a student still expecting it to continue.
interrupts.why: A transfer already underway does not pause for an unrelated call across the room — the safest response is finishing the step in front of you with your full attention, then responding, because a lift or pivot left half-finished to answer something else is exactly when a student who trusted the hold gets dropped.
interrupts.wrongNote: Stay on the gait belt — the transfer in front of you finishes before anything else gets your attention.

lateNotes.brace-effort: The pivot happens once the count of three has actually been called — that's the next step.
lateNotes.gait-belt: Not yet — the belt goes on once the pre-lift check has actually cleared the space, not before.

name: Paraeducator Safe Lift & Transfer

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Read the student's individualized transfer plan before touching anything.
steps.prompt: Read the student's individualized transfer plan before touching anything.
steps.title: Read today's transfer plan
steps.why: The plan names the technique, the equipment and the number of staff this specific transfer calls for, and it can change as a student's needs change — reading it fresh, every time, is what keeps a paraeducator from running yesterday's transfer on a plan that's since been updated.

steps.cue: Use the intercom to tell the classroom teacher the transfer is beginning.
steps.prompt: Use the intercom to tell the classroom teacher the transfer is beginning.
steps.title: Let the classroom teacher know the transfer is starting
steps.why: The classroom teacher is running the rest of the room during this transfer and needs to know two adults are about to be occupied with it — a quick heads-up is what keeps the teacher from expecting a paraeducator's attention on anything else for the next few minutes.

steps.cue: Lock the wheelchair's brakes, set the transfer board in position, then clear the path to the classroom chair, in that order.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Brakes, then the board, then the path — the chair has to be locked down before either the board or the path matters.
steps.prompt: Lock the wheelchair's brakes, set the transfer board in position, then clear the path to the classroom chair, in that order.
steps.title: Lock the brakes, ready the board, clear the path
steps.why: The brakes are locked before anything else because every step after this one assumes the chair isn't moving; the path gets cleared last so nothing that was in the way during setup is still there once the actual lift starts.

steps.cue: Hold the brake lever fully engaged and confirm it clicks locked on both sides.
steps.holdBreakNote: You let go before both sides clicked locked. A brake that isn't confirmed locked is a chair that might still roll under a lift.
steps.prompt: Hold the brake lever fully engaged and confirm it clicks locked on both sides.
steps.title: Confirm the brakes are actually locked
steps.why: A brake lever that looks engaged and one that's actually clicked into its locked position are not always the same thing — holding it to the click on both sides is what turns 'probably locked' into a chair that's certain not to roll.

steps.cue: Three things about this room are not right. Find them before the count of three.

itemNames.obstruction-in-path: the chair left in the transfer path

itemNotes.loose-gait-belt-buckle: This gait belt's buckle isn't fully seated. A belt that isn't seated can let go under load at the exact moment it's needed to hold weight.
itemNotes.obstruction-in-path: A stray chair is sitting in the transfer path between the wheelchair and the classroom seat. Anything in that path is something a paraeducator mid-pivot, watching the student rather than the floor, can catch a foot on.
itemNotes.unlocked-brake-lever: A second wheelchair nearby has its brake lever sitting unlocked. It isn't the chair being transferred from today, but an unlocked chair anywhere in a room used for transfers is one more thing that can roll into the space at the wrong moment.

steps.prompt: Three things about this room are not right. Find them before the count of three.
steps.title: Walk the room before the lift
steps.why: The room gets checked the same way the wheelchair's own brakes do — assumed right is not the same as confirmed right, and every one of these three problems is easiest to catch standing still, before two people are mid-lift and looking at each other instead of the floor.

steps.cue: Fit the gait belt snugly at the waist and check it seats fully.
steps.prompt: Fit the gait belt snugly at the waist and check it seats fully.
steps.title: Fit the gait belt
steps.why: The gait belt is the one hold in this whole transfer built to carry weight safely — fitted snugly and fully seated, it gives both paraeducators a grip that won't slip or pull on a joint the way an arm or an underarm hold can.

steps.cue: Confirm your partner is braced and ready on the other side before the count.
steps.prompt: Confirm your partner is braced and ready on the other side before the count.
steps.title: Confirm the second paraeducator is in position
steps.why: The plan calls for two people specifically because a transfer that starts to go wrong needs a second set of hands already in place — checking your partner is set, out loud, before the count is what makes this a two-person lift in practice and not just on paper.

steps.cue: Keep your own effort steady through the pivot — braced through the legs, not the back.
steps.holdBreakNote: Effort out of band — too little risks losing control of the pivot, too much means the back just took over from the legs. Bring it back to steady.
steps.prompt: Keep your own effort steady through the pivot — braced through the legs, not the back.
steps.title: Hold a braced, steady pivot
steps.why: A pivot done right loads the legs at a steady, sustained effort and turns on the feet; one done wrong spikes as the back takes over mid-lift, exactly the moment a twisted spine is loaded hardest — holding a steady band the whole way through is what keeps the legs doing the work the back cannot do safely.

steps.cue: Guide the student down into the classroom chair, aligned and settled.

drag.missNote: Not aligned in the chair yet. Settle the student fully into the seat before letting go of the belt.

steps.prompt: Guide the student down into the classroom chair, aligned and settled.
steps.title: Settle the student into the classroom chair
steps.why: The pivot only finishes once the student is actually seated and aligned in the new chair — set down off-centre or at an angle, and the transfer isn't complete no matter how well the lift itself went.

steps.cue: Wheel the chair clear and turn the brake lever to lock it in its parking spot.
steps.prompt: Wheel the chair clear and turn the brake lever to lock it in its parking spot.
steps.title: Park and re-lock the empty wheelchair
steps.why: An empty wheelchair left unlocked in a busy classroom is its own rolling hazard — parking it clear of the walkway and locking it again is what keeps it exactly where it was left until it's needed for the next transfer.

steps.cue: Hold the buckle closed until it clicks fully seated.
steps.holdBreakNote: The buckle didn't click fully seated before you let go. A belt that isn't seated does nothing the moment it's actually needed.
steps.prompt: Hold the buckle closed until it clicks fully seated.
steps.title: Fasten the seatbelt in the new seat
steps.why: A transfer that ends with the student unsecured in the new seat has only moved the risk from the lift itself to the first time that chair shifts or tips — the seatbelt closes out the transfer, not the pivot.

steps.cue: Record the time, the technique used and how the student tolerated it.
steps.prompt: Record the time, the technique used and how the student tolerated it.
steps.title: Log the transfer
steps.why: The log is what tells the next paraeducator, the case manager or the family whether this transfer went the way the plan expects — a change in how a student tolerates the lift is exactly the kind of thing that has to show up here before it shows up as a bigger problem.

supportLine: your AFT or CSEA chapter's member assistance line, or the district's employee assistance programme
